abstract: Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) transcriptomic studies have generated diverse datasets across parental lineages, cell-line development histories, and culture conditions. However, the transcriptional programs underlying this heterogeneity remain difficult to compare and interpret across studies. Here, we asked whether heterogeneous CHO transcriptomes could be organized into reproducible and biologically interpretable transcriptional modules. To address this, we assembled a discovery compendium of 778 quality-controlled RNA-seq samples spanning multiple parental lineages, engineered cell backgrounds, culture conditions, and perturbations, and applied robust multi-run independent component analysis, resulting in 105 independently modulated gene sets, termed iModulons. To accommodate mammalian regulatory and genomic complexity, we interpreted these modules by integrating gene function, activity-metadata associations, promoter motifs, genomic localization, and RNA-biotype composition. The iModulons captured lineage-associated variation, chromosomal enrichment, and responses to temperature downshift and antiviral stimulation, together with an ATF4-associated amino-acid-stress program. Projection of 377 independent samples onto the discovery-derived iModulons reproduced selected lineage- and process-associated activity patterns and captured a glutamine-deprivation response not represented in the discovery compendium, supporting the transferability of these modules across datasets. When the compendium was expanded to 1,155 samples and ICA was repeated de novo, 89 of the 105 discovery iModulons were preserved among 148 expanded modules, while an additional CHO-DXB11-associated transcriptional pattern emerged. To our knowledge, this study represents the first application of the iModulon framework to a mammalian cell system, establishing a transferable and expandable set of transcriptional coordinates for comparing CHO cell states across heterogeneous datasets and prioritizing programs relevant to cell-line and bioprocess engineering.
